newsitem.title: USA: Alleged China foray in U.S. politics seen as naive.
newsitem.headline: Alleged China foray in U.S. politics seen as naive.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent
Allegations that China tried to give campaign donations to U.S. politicians have added an explosive hint of possible covert foreign subversion to a growing scandal over campaign finances.

Analysts interviewed by Reuters, however, said the Chinese attempt, if it indeed happened, was more clumsy and naive than sinister and may have grown out of a fundamental Chinese misunderstanding of how the U.S. political system works.
"Either this is China being nefarious or China being naive and clumsy. I tend towards naive and clumsy," said Janet Heininger, a China scholar at the American University.
"They don't have the foggiest idea of how U.S. democracy works, but we are often just as clumsy dealing with them as they are with us," she said.

Gary Jacobson of the University of California, San Diego, said: "It's possible they extrapolated from their own political culture that it's important to give gifts to people with whom you want to do business."

The allegations came to light last weekend when the Washington Post reported that the FBI warned six members of Congress last year they had been targeted by China to receive illegal campaign contributions, said to total some $2 million. The Justice Department is investigating the allegations.
It is illegal to accept campaign donations from foreign governments, corporations or citizens.
China heatedly denied the report and accused the United States of damaging relations between the two nations.

"Such slanderous news and reports about China are ill-motivated fabrications ... We hereby express our indignation and strong displeasure,"said Mei Ping, director of the Chinese Foreign Ministry's Americas department.

Vice President Al Gore is due to visit China this month on a mission to improve relations and prepare for a summit later this year. Now, with mutual suspicions growing, that task has become more difficult and China's position on Capitol Hill is likely to weaken even further.

Republicans seized on the issue to embarrass President Bill Clinton, suggesting that China was trying to buy the White House. They again focused on the activities of John Huang, the former Democratic Party and Commerce Department official whose fund raising last year from Asian business interests is already under investigation.

"When you have John Huang in the White House 94 times ... what was done there? Why did he have security clearance? He had security clearance before he went to Congress ... He visited the Chinese Embassy, he visited the Indonesian Embassy," said Sen. Don Nickles, an Oklahoma Republican.

Sen. Orrin Hatch, a Utah Republican, added: "Remember when (then-first lady) Nancy Reagan got so criticised by the media for asking outside people to purchase the White House china? ... Here we have China trying to purchase the White House."

However, the $2 million China was allegedly prepared to devote to the project was pocket money in an environment, where the Republicans raised $550 million and the Democrats $330 million in the past two years.

Sino-American relations have been plagued by tensions for years. China bristles at U.S. criticism of its human rights record, its trading practices and some of its sales of sophisticated military technology to Third World nations.

Beijing would like to be spared the annual debate over whether to extend its most favoured nation trading status. It would like Washington to open the door to its membership of international institutions such as the World Trade Organisation and it would like U.S. politicians to stop cozying up to Taiwan.

On the American side, many politicians resent China's attitude towards Taiwan, and more recently Hong Kong, and are disturbed by its treatment of dissidents, prisoners, workers, Christians and Tibetans.

If China had simply used its $2 million to set up a lobbying organisation in Washington, no one would have raised an eyebrow because it would have been playing the game in the same way as other foreign countries seeking to promote their interests with Congress. Taiwan has a particularly active and effective lobby in Washington.

U.S. corporations with interests in China have long urged Beijing to follow suit. But it has balked at spending the kind of money a sophisticated lobbying operation needs and is reluctant to let non-Chinese argue its case in Washington.
